task_row_model.query: A 62-year-old patient has long-standing refractory hypertension on three agents and episodic headaches, diaphoresis and palpitations. Plasma free metanephrines were elevated on one sample but an abdominal MRI did not show an obvious adrenal mass. How should I confirm diagnosis of pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma, proceed with tumor localization when extra-adrenal disease is suspected, which genetic tests should be offered, and what is the recommended preoperative pharmacologic preparation including timing, targets, and intraoperative considerations?

documents.content: Imaging for suspected pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma should be tailored to biochemical findings and suspected tumor location. First-line anatomic imaging is contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen/pelvis or MRI when CT is contraindicated; MRI is preferred for head and neck and for younger patients to reduce radiation. If an adrenal or extra-adrenal lesion is not found or multifocal/metastatic disease is a concern, proceed to functional imaging: 123I-MIBG scintigraphy can detect catecholamine-secreting tumors, 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT is highly sensitive for somatostatin-receptor–positive paragangliomas, 18F-FDOPA PET is useful for many sporadic tumors and head/neck lesions, and 18F-FDG PET is particularly sensitive for SDHB-related metastatic disease.
documents.reasoning_trace: Outlined imaging hierarchy: start with anatomic CT/MRI, noted MRI preference for head/neck and radiation avoidance. Listed available functional modalities and their typical indications, emphasizing sequence: anatomic first, then targeted nuclear modalities for extra-adrenal or metastatic suspicion.

documents.content: Biochemical testing is the first diagnostic step for suspected pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma. Plasma free metanephrines have the highest sensitivity; collect samples after the patient has been supine for at least 20–30 minutes to reduce false positives. A 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrine and catecholamine profile is an alternative or confirmatory test. Be aware of common false-positive causes: certain antidepressants, sympathomimetics, some antiemetics, recent exercise, and acute illness. When initial results are borderline, a clonidine suppression test can help distinguish sympathetic activation from tumor-related catecholamine excess.
documents.reasoning_trace: Focused on biochemical strategy: emphasized proper sampling conditions, sensitivity of plasma free metanephrines, role of 24-hour urine, medication and physiologic confounders, and the clonidine suppression test for indeterminate results.

documents.content: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) is an important cause of secondary hypertension characterized by hypokalemia and an elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio. Screening requires measurement of plasma renin activity (or direct renin concentration) and plasma aldosterone with the patient on an appropriate medication regimen; interfering agents should be adjusted before testing. Confirmatory testing includes oral sodium loading, saline infusion test, or fludrocortisone suppression. Localization of aldosterone-producing adenomas versus bilateral hyperplasia often requires CT imaging followed by adrenal venous sampling when imaging and clinical data are discordant.
documents.reasoning_trace: Wrote a concise overview of primary hyperaldosteronism: pathophysiology, screening labs, confirmatory suppression tests, and the role of adrenal venous sampling for localization when CT is inconclusive.

documents.content: Confirm pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma (PPGL) by first obtaining properly collected biochemical tests: plasma free metanephrines with the patient supine after 20–30 minutes or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines. If results are equivocal, perform a clonidine suppression test or repeat testing off interfering medications where safe. For localization after biochemical confirmation, start with CT abdomen/pelvis or MRI (MRI preferred for head/neck and younger patients). If no lesion is seen or extra-adrenal disease is suspected, proceed to functional imaging: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT for somatostatin-receptor–positive paragangliomas, 18F-FDOPA PET for many head/neck tumors, 123I-MIBG for classical adrenal pheochromocytoma, and 18F-FDG PET particularly for SDHB-associated or metastatic disease. Offer germline genetic testing to all patients given the high prevalence of pathogenic variants; prioritize testing for SDHB, SDHD, VHL, RET, NF1 and others based on phenotype, age, and family history. Preoperative preparation: initiate alpha-adrenergic blockade (phenoxybenzamine or a selective alpha-1 blocker such as doxazosin) for 7–14 days, achieve adequate blood pressure control and orthostatic tolerance, encourage salt and fluid intake to expand intravascular volume, and add a beta-blocker only after adequate alpha blockade if tachycardia persists. In refractory or large tumors consider metyrosine to reduce catecholamine synthesis. Intraoperatively plan for invasive hemodynamic monitoring, short-acting vasodilators for hypertensive surges, and vasopressors for post-resection hypotension.
documents.reasoning_trace: Integrated diagnostic, localization, genetic, and perioperative management steps: included specimen collection details, anatomic then functional imaging sequence with modality-specific indications, rationale for offering germline testing and key genes, and detailed preoperative pharmacologic strategy including timing, volume expansion, beta-blockade sequencing, and intraoperative monitoring and agents.

documents.content: Management of hypertensive emergency focuses on rapid but controlled blood pressure reduction to limit end-organ damage. Use intravenous agents with short titratable effects such as nicardipine, sodium nitroprusside, or labetalol depending on the clinical scenario; avoid excessive drops in perfusion pressure. Target pressures and agents differ by condition: acute aortic dissection requires rapid systolic reduction to <120 mm Hg, acute ischemic stroke has more conservative thresholds, and hypertensive encephalopathy benefits from gradual lowering. Continuous monitoring in an ICU or step-down unit is recommended, along with evaluation for secondary causes if resistant hypertension is suspected.
documents.reasoning_trace: Summarized general principles of hypertensive emergency management: choice of IV agents, condition-specific targets, need for controlled reduction and continuous monitoring, and consideration of secondary causes in resistant cases.
